newsitem.title: USA: Brooke enters settlement with Calif..
newsitem.headline: Brooke enters settlement with Calif..

text.p: Brooke Group Ltd said on Thursday that it has entered a settlement in principle with California to resolve the state's Medicaid reimbursement claims over tobacco-related illnesses.
Brooke Group said the agreement with California is with substantially the same terms as the previous agreement the company made with 22 other states.

By settling with California, the most populous state which accounts for approximately 20 percent of the country's Medicaid claims, Brooke now has resolved approximately 70 percent of Medicaid claims nationwide, Brooke Group said.

Brooke, the parent company of Liggett, said it has also reached a separate settlement in principle with San Francisco and 10 surrounding counties regarding to production of documents and other elements related to tobacco industry lawsuits.
The separate deal with San Francisco and the counties does not entail any monetary payments, Brooke said.

Liggett has agreed to place warnings on its cigarettes stating that "smoking is addictive" and that it will pay 25 percent of its pretax income for the next 25 years into a settlement fund to compensate state health care programs and fund counter-market advertising, Brooke Group said.
California Attorney General Dan Lungren said in a statement, "This historic settlement is extraordinary in that California did not even have to sue Liggett in order to strike this agreement."

"California also gains access to internal tobacco company documents that may provide evidence that the industry targeted minors with its advertising, manipulated nicotine levels and/ or engaged in illegal, fraudulent conduct," Lungren said.
Brooke's Liggett broke ranks with other cigarette makers to enter this settlement, acknowledge that smoking is addictive, and provide documents.
Rival cigarette companies claim that the documents are subject to attorney-client privilege.
Lungren said that he does not expect other tobacco companies to voluntarily enter a settlement.

California is precluded from pursuing litigation against tobacco companies due to a state law passed in 1987 that specifically exempted tobacco companies from liability for injuries caused by tobacco, Lungren said.
Lungren has requested that California's legislature repeal the exemption.
